Using power responsibly

If you could control everything, should you?

Being able to control something does not settle whether you should.

A closer lookOpen in a larger view ↗

The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

A philosophical and theological argument

Kenosis is a Christian word often translated as “self-emptying.” Here it means choosing to use power in ways that give others room to act, rather than taking over their choices.

Making room does not mean leaving people unprotected. If one person is taking away another’s freedom, care may require a boundary or an intervention. Ask whose freedom your restraint protects, and whose needs it may overlook.

This is a philosophical and theological argument. It is not a scientific rule or an instruction about your own relationships.

Words used here
kenosis
A Christian term often translated as “self-emptying.” Here it means using power while making room for others to act.
agency
A person’s ability to make choices and have a meaningful effect on what happens.
Read the fuller explanation

Kenosis asks how power can make room for another person’s agency. Restraint, trust and formation matter. So do protection and responsibility.

The difficult boundary is where restraint permits one person to destroy another’s effective agency. Care can require intervention.

Where this comes from: Power, restraint and responsibility

Theological and philosophical argument

A philosophical and theological argument

Distinguishes the ability to use power from permission and responsibility. It makes room for both restraint and protection. It is not a scientific law.

Kenotic governance and shared responsibility

Capability, moral permission and an obligation to exercise power are distinguished. Restraint must also be examined where one agent destroys another’s effective agency. The argument remains defeasible and is not a physical derivation.
